subtitle: Describing a graph, and four precise little words
words.intro: Frankfurt’s stock exchange has a bull and a bear outside, and a very big board inside. Germans are famous savers, and they talk about money more readily as a line going up or down than as a sum.

grammar[0].fact: German exams and job interviews have a standard task: *Beschreiben Sie die Grafik*. There’s a standard order too: source, subject, main trend, details, then a reason. The university entrance test for foreigners has been asking for it for decades.

grammar[1].blocks[1].title: Rising formality
grammar[1].blocks[1].note: All of them send the verb to the end — except Insofern hast du recht.
grammar[1].blocks[2].title: Words for the practice page
grammar[1].fact: *Zumal* is a favourite: it adds a reason on top of the reasons you’ve already given. *Ich komme nicht, zumal ich krank bin.* It has a slight edge of triumph. Save it for when you’ve already won.

document.intro: A real savings-bank statement from December 1990, from just after the East’s money became West German marks. It’s the shortest graph there is: two numbers, old and new. *Saldo* is the balance.
document.fact: On 1 July 1990 East Germans exchanged their savings for West German marks, most of it at one to one. People queued overnight outside banks. Slips like this one were among the first things that changed in their lives.

reading.intro: Max has a new job in Frankfurt, presenting numbers. On Monday the whole board wants a graph of last year’s sales. Max has made one on Lena’s laptop the night before. Herr Dr. Blum, the chairman, peers at the screen. It’s the wrong graph.
reading.photos[1].caption: Der Bulle vor der Börse: Wenn er gut gelaunt ist, steigen die Kurse.
reading.fact: Germans keep an unusual share of their savings in cash and bank accounts rather than in shares. *Die Aktie* is viewed with suspicion by many since a state telecoms flotation lost small savers a fortune around 2000. The phrase *Spare in der Zeit, so hast du in der Not* is taught early.
